# Slack integration (`pyrunner_integrations.slack`)

Slack for scripts: post and update messages, upload files, list channels, read a channel's messages and list people.

The connection is a Slack app installed in your Slack workspace: its bot token
(`xoxb-...`), pasted or through Connect. Each function needs the app to have
the matching scope (the boxes on the connection form): `chat:write` to post
and update, `files:write` to upload, `channels:read` to list channels,
`channels:history` to read messages, `users:read` to list people. The bot
posts only in channels it is a member of: invite it first (`/invite @your-app`),
or Slack answers `not_in_channel`.

A channel is its id (`C0123ABCD`; in Slack: the channel's name, then "Copy
link" or the About tab) or, where a function says so, its name (`#general`).
Messages are Slack's own dicts (`ts`, `text`, `user`...): a message's
`ts` is its id, which `update_message` and `thread_ts` take.
Lists come page by page as you read them; `limit` stops early.

## Connection

It uses a connection of the **Slack** kind (provider `slack`), which signs in with OAuth (Connect or a pasted token). Add one under **Connections** in the sidebar and grant it to the script. Every function takes `connection=`: the connection's name, or nothing for the script's one `slack` connection.

The credentials go only to the connection's base URL; a redirect elsewhere goes on without them.

## Example

```python
from pyrunner_integrations import slack

# A message, then a reply in its thread (the app must be in #alerts: /invite @your-app).
sent = slack.post_message("#alerts", "*Disk almost full* on web-1 (92%)")
slack.post_message("#alerts", "Cleaned up the logs: 61% now.", thread_ts=sent["ts"])

# Edit the first message once it is handled.
slack.update_message(sent["channel"], sent["ts"], ":white_check_mark: Disk on web-1 back to 61%")

# A file, shared in a channel with a comment.
slack.upload_file("/tmp/report.csv", "#reports", comment="This week's signups")

# The last messages of a channel (by id), newest first.
for message in slack.history("C0123ABCD", limit=10):
    print(message["ts"], message.get("text"))
```

## Functions

### post_message

```python
slack.post_message(channel, text=None, *, blocks=None, thread_ts=None, reply_broadcast=False, unfurl_links=None, connection=None)
```

Post a message and return `{"channel", "ts", "message"}` (`ts` is the new message's id).

`channel` is a channel's id or name (`#general`), or a person's user id
(`U0123ABCD`) for a direct message from the app. `text` takes Slack's
markup (`*bold*`, `<https://example.com|a link>`, `<@U0123ABCD>`);
`blocks` is a list of Block Kit blocks (then `text` is the notification's
fallback). `thread_ts` replies in that message's thread
(`reply_broadcast=True` also shows it in the channel). `unfurl_links=False`
turns off link previews. Needs `chat:write`. For example:

```python
sent = slack.post_message("#alerts", "*Disk almost full* on web-1")
slack.post_message("#alerts", "Cleaned up: 40 GB free.", thread_ts=sent["ts"])
```

### update_message

```python
slack.update_message(channel, ts, text=None, *, blocks=None, connection=None)
```

Change a message the app posted (its `ts`) and return `{"channel", "ts", "text", "message"}`.

`channel` is the channel's id (as `post_message` returned it). Needs
`chat:write`. For example:

```python
sent = slack.post_message("#deploys", "Deploying v2.5...")
slack.update_message(sent["channel"], sent["ts"], "Deployed v2.5 :white_check_mark:")
```

### upload_file

```python
slack.upload_file(file, channel=None, *, filename=None, title=None, comment=None, thread_ts=None, alt_text=None, connection=None)
```

Upload a file (a path, or bytes with `filename=`) and return Slack's file `{"id", "title"}`.

With `channel` (an id, or a public channel's name `#reports`) it is
shared there, with `comment` as its message, in `thread_ts`'s thread when
given; without, it stays private to the app until shared. `alt_text`
describes an image. Uses Slack's three-step upload (an upload URL, the
file sent there without the token, then completing it). Needs
`files:write` (and `channels:read` for a channel's name). The file is
read into memory whole (Slack takes up to 1 GB). For example:

```python
slack.upload_file("/tmp/report.pdf", "#reports", comment="This week's numbers")
slack.upload_file(csv_text.encode(), "C0123ABCD", filename="leads.csv")
```

### list_channels

```python
slack.list_channels(*, types='public_channel', include_archived=False, limit=None, connection=None)
```

Yield the workspace's channels: Slack's channel dicts (`id`, `name`, `is_member`, `topic`...).

`types` is a comma-separated list of `public_channel`,
`private_channel` (needs `groups:read`), `mpim` (`mpim:read`) and
`im` (`im:read`). Archived
channels are left out unless `include_archived=True`. Needs
`channels:read`. For example:

```python
for channel in slack.list_channels():
    print(channel["id"], channel["name"], "member" if channel["is_member"] else "")
```

### find_channel

```python
slack.find_channel(name, *, types='public_channel', connection=None)
```

The channel named `name` (with or without `#`), or None. Needs `channels:read`.

For example:

```python
alerts = slack.find_channel("#alerts")
if alerts and not alerts["is_member"]:
    print("Invite the app to #alerts first")
```

### history

```python
slack.history(channel, *, oldest=None, latest=None, limit=None, connection=None)
```

Yield a channel's messages, newest first: Slack's message dicts (`ts`, `user`, `text`...).

`channel` is the channel's id. `oldest` / `latest` are message
`ts` values (or Unix times) bounding the messages returned (both
excluded). Thread replies stay in their threads. Needs
`channels:history` (`groups:history` for a private channel). For example:

```python
for message in slack.history("C0123ABCD", limit=20):
    print(message["ts"], message.get("user"), message.get("text"))
```

### list_users

```python
slack.list_users(*, include_bots=False, include_deleted=False, limit=None, connection=None)
```

Yield the workspace's people: Slack's user dicts (`id`, `name`, `real_name`, `profile`...).

Bots and deactivated accounts are left out unless asked for. Needs
`users:read` (`users:read.email` for `profile["email"]`). For example:

```python
names = {user["id"]: user["real_name"] for user in slack.list_users()}
```

### client

```python
slack.client(connection=None, *, timeout=30)
```

The shared client of `connection`, for Slack methods this module has no function for.

Paths are method names under `https://slack.com/api`; a reply with
`"ok": false` raises, as in the functions here. For example:

```python
slack.client().post("/reactions.add", json={"channel": channel, "timestamp": ts, "name": "eyes"})
```

## Errors

Every function raises `pyrunner_integrations.IntegrationError` (a `pyrunner_connections.ConnectionsError`, so one `except` catches both) with `code`, `status` (the HTTP status, or None) and `retry_after` (seconds, or None). Its message never holds the connection's credentials. Before raising, the client retries a 429 (or a 503 with Retry-After) up to 3 times, waiting what the service asks (up to 60 s; longer, and the error says it in `retry_after`) or else 1, 2 or 4 seconds; other 5xx replies and lost connections only for GET, PUT, DELETE and other calls that are safe to repeat. After a 401 it asks PyRun once for new credentials (an OAuth token is refreshed then) and tries again.

Slack answers most failures with HTTP 200 and `"ok": false`: those raise too, with the code below and Slack's error name in the message and in the exception's `slack_error` (`not_in_channel` is FORBIDDEN, `channel_not_found` NOT_FOUND, `missing_scope` FORBIDDEN naming the scope it needs). After `invalid_auth` or `token_expired` PyRun is asked once for new credentials, as after a 401.

| Code | When |
|---|---|
| `INVALID_REQUEST` | The service refused the request as malformed (HTTP 400, 405 or 422). |
| `UNAUTHORIZED` | The service refused the credentials (HTTP 401), also after PyRun was asked for new ones. |
| `FORBIDDEN` | The account may not do this (HTTP 403): a missing scope or permission. |
| `NOT_FOUND` | No such thing (HTTP 404 or 410). |
| `CONFLICT` | It clashes with the current state (HTTP 409 or 412). |
| `RATE_LIMITED` | Too many requests (HTTP 429), still after the retries; `retry_after` says when to try again. |
| `HTTP_ERROR` | Any other 4xx reply. |
| `SERVER_ERROR` | The service failed (HTTP 5xx), still after the retries. |
| `UNREACHABLE` | The service couldn't be reached (DNS, refused connection, TLS). |
| `TIMEOUT` | No reply in time. |
| `BAD_RESPONSE` | A reply that can't be used: broken JSON, too many redirects or pages, a repeated page cursor. |
| `NOT_HTTP` | The connection isn't an HTTP connection (an SMTP login). |
| `SLACK_ERROR` | Slack refused the call with an error none of the codes above covers; `slack_error` holds Slack's own name for it (`cant_update_message`, `is_archived`...). |
| `CONNECTION_...` | The connection can't be used: `CONNECTION_NOT_FOUND`, `CONNECTION_EXPIRED`... (see [Connections](../run-context.md#connections)). |
